data.title: How Malaysia’s QR payments boom is shaping Singapore’s PayNow Gen 2
data.description:
Sustainable economics for all is the condition that makes it work, industry players say.

Opening up Malaysia’s largest payment merchant network to all competitors felt like a setback, until it drove 60% annual QR growth for five years and made credit and debit cards an afterthought.

Alan Ni, CEO of TNG Digital, described the moment Bank Negara Malaysia directed his company to open its two-million-strong SME merchant base to every issuer, wallet, and bank for free, roughly four to five years ago. At the time, TNG Digital was the largest SME merchant acquirer in Malaysia.

“Sounds like a very bad thing,” Ni said during a panel discussion at the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026. “But now five years later, in hindsight, it might be the best thing ever happened to us.”

QR payments in Malaysia grew at around 60% annually over the five years that followed. In 2025, QR payments surpassed both credit card and debit card transactions in Malaysia by value and volume. Ni attributed the growth directly to interoperability: because TNG Digital had to open to everyone, everyone had to open to TNG Digital in return.

Losing the merchant network as a competitive moat pushed the company to find new ways to deliver value-added services, he said.

The experience resonates in Singapore. Jo Yeo, director at MAS who moderated the session, said Singapore has drawn inspiration from that model in building a possible switch under PayNow Generation 2 to enable interoperability across users, including visitors to Singapore, and the merchant base. 

Lawrence Chan, group CEO of NETS Singapore, who contributed to the PayNow Generation 2 report on the interoperable switch, said in practical terms that means any licensed payment app, domestic or inbound, would be able to scan any QR code. Merchants that previously needed multiple contracts to accept different payment apps would need only one acquiring relationship.

Chan identified two requirements for interoperability to succeed. The first is consistent user experience, so that the payment works every time it promises to. The second is sustainable economics for all participants in the ecosystem.

“The economics needs to be there to ensure that it’s sustainable over time,” he said. “We don’t want just to pilot. We want to make it work now, and potentially keep on improving on it over time.”

Carrie Suen, vice president and head of global affairs at Ant International, said the same tension plays out at a global scale. Alipay Plus connects 53 super apps across 150 million merchants in 200 markets and works with close to 15 national payment rails. She said technology has become relatively easier to manage, but governance and commercial sustainability remain the harder challenges.

“Moving money, moving data across borders still remain a challenge,” she said.

She identified three elements that must exist for global connectivity to scale: common technical operating standards, clear accountability frameworks, and commercially sustainable incentives for all participants. 

“We need to find a balance where that commercial arrangement also reflect the value creation and the risk responsibilities across all the actors within the chain,” she said.

Ni drew the clearest lesson from TNG Digital’s experience. If regulators focus only on frameworks whilst pushing commercial margins to unsustainable levels, private sector players will disengage and the ecosystem will not function.

“If the regulator stop at only doing the regulatory framework, and totally forget about commercial, or maybe push the commercial to very very low, which is unsustainable. Then you will miss the participation from the private sector. Then this won’t work,” he said.

Chan said the commitment shown so far gives him confidence that more is possible. 

“With further commitment to work with each other, to find the right balance, to find the right economics, to find the right user experience, to find the right safety and security, definitely, we can serve more,” he said.

data.title: Why agentic AI alone will not improve banks without internal change
data.description:
DBS combined its corporate and consumer call centers due to chatbots’ impact in their processes.

Slapping an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) tool in your banking business isn’t going to automatically improve your business—processes and cultures must also be changed, banking experts said.

Derrick Go, group chief operating officer at DBS, said that in order to properly leverage AI banks will need to modernise their technology architecture, consider data quality, and change the way that teams collaborate within an organisation.

DBS, for example, created a chatbot to bring down the volume of calls fielded by its 1,600 call center staff worldwide, Go told attendees of the panel “How Can Agentic AI Create a Commercial and Competitive Advantage?” at the FutureMatters Stage of Singapore Fintech Festival 2026, 18 November.

Through this, DBS was able to combine its corporate and consumer call center, Go said, which he said enabled the bank to cut costs and keep customers happier as it provides quicker answers for their more complex questions.

“[The call center staff] can do a lot more than what they used to do. They can answer more complex questions than what they used to do, especially those in our consumer call centers. So we are making them pick up corporate calls as well,” Go said in the panel, which was moderated by Pat Patel, managing director, forums, at GFTN.

Melvyn Low, group strategy & transformation officer at OCBC, said that the real opportunity in AI is how it unlocked new ways of thinking within the organisation, from new ways of working to new business models to news products.

“You have to deploy the technology where it's needed to improve your efficiency, but you also have to think about the technology in the context of the world today,” Low said.

Low said that AI must have the right context to operate. He advised businesses to question why processes are done a certain way.

“If you don't understand your processes and why you were doing it, and the common phrase of ‘but we've done this all along’, right, it is not something that you should be looking at. You need to understand why you do something in a certain way, and there's probably many reasons for it,” Low said.

Carson Pickens, global head of data & intelligence for FIS, said that organisations should not shy away from using agentic AI in highly regulated use cases. The most regulated use cases will have the most standard operating procedures and the most documentation, Pickens said.

“Even though they might carry the most risk, they also carry the most context to allow you to effectively build things without having to do all the process mining and process engineering,” Pickens said.

Namrata Jolly, managing director and head of FSI Asia for Microsoft, circled back to Go’s point that using AI does not automatically translate to business value.

Jolly noted how Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) reduced fraud losses by 20% by having AI monitor and scan the 80 million events and 20 million payments it processes daily; and how Northern Trust used agentic AI to bring down client onboard to two days from the previous two and a half weeks’ turnaround time.

Jolly also emphasized building the right culture in an organisation of moving fast, as well as governance.

“You can have the models, right? But you have to have smart drivers. You have to have good fuel, and you also have to have a very good braking system. If you have the right brakes,you can go as fast as required,” she said.

Low said that beyond all, people will be the biggest differentiator in determining the competitive and commercial advantage that agentic AI offers.

“I say people because the source of competitive advantage is proprietary knowledge,” Low said. He cited a recent hackathon by OCBC, where he said the bank was amazed to find that its employees have ideas for the bank’s other divisions, places, and areas of business.

“What it taught me was that if you invest in the right way with your people, give them the right tools, guardrail them within the organization so that you don't lose anything. You probably get the best competitive advantage,” Low said.

data.title: Regulatory gaps still block scale for live stablecoins
data.description:
International accounting rules treat them as investments rather than cash, according to Societe Generale-FORGE.

Regulated stablecoins are operational and finding use cases, but a range of unresolved regulatory questions is preventing them from scaling.

Societe Generale-FORGE, a subsidiary of Societe Generale dedicated to digital assets, has been working on digital assets for six years, issuing tokenised bonds from 2019. For the past two years, it has issued two stablecoins: a euro and a US dollar stablecoin, both called coinvertible and regulated under MiCA.

Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival, Chief Strategy and Global Policy Officer Stephanie Cabossioras said the firm was amongst the first major banking entities in the world to issue stablecoins. It was also the first to receive a MiCA licence in Europe for stablecoin issuance, in July 2024.

“Every time we want to develop a use case, there’s always a legal blocker somewhere,” she said.

The blockers are concrete and varied. For international companies, regulated stablecoins are not treated as cash equivalents under IFRS but as investment products, adding accounting friction for corporates that want to hold them. France has updated its accounting norms to treat MiCA-regulated stablecoins as cash equivalents, but that change applies only under French norms and has not been adopted under IFRS for large international companies.

Investment funds present a separate obstacle. Tokenised investment fund shares are emerging, but buyers cannot use stablecoins to purchase them without the fund off-ramping to fiat intraday, meaning the fund cannot hold stablecoins as a settlement asset.

For central counterparties, stablecoins could address a specific need. Using them for margin calls and collateral management would allow collateral to move instantly, reducing the amount immobilised as guarantee whilst awaiting settlement. CCP regulation in Europe, however, makes no mention of blockchain, creating legal uncertainty that is only beginning to be addressed.

Stablecoins are also not recognised as high-quality liquid assets for prudential purposes, adding further friction for institutions.

“We don’t believe that this new technology will change fundamentally the business drivers, but it will change the infrastructure, the technology,” Cabossioras said. “It’s really a challenge for incumbents, for financial institutions, for big banks to accompany this change, to offer that to our clients.”

On the central bank side, wholesale CBDC infrastructure is already moving. Dr. Alexandra Hachmeister, director general Digital Euro at Deutsche Bundesbank, said the euro system has been running a full production environment for wholesale CBDC transactions since end of September, with market participants already testing different transaction types including large issuances. 

She said the next step is for the asset side to truly tokenise at scale.

Cabossioras said the firm is working on several fronts. Use cases include crypto market infrastructure, bringing regulated assets into refinancing, repo, and collateral management, and cross-border payments, including a corridor with Asia.

The firm has developed partnerships with central securities depositories including Clearstream and Euroclear, as well as SWIFT, with the aim of integrating stablecoins as a cash leg for securities settlement. That work is not yet live, and regulatory frameworks still need to evolve to support it.

Cabossioras said the underlying belief driving the firm’s work is structural.

“The banking infrastructure layer, post-market payment infrastructure will progressively move to DLT, decentralised infrastructure, blockchain infrastructures, just for one reason, because it allows instant transfer of value all around the world,” she said.

She said the most urgent near-term need from the industry is for all financial institutions to build wallet infrastructure for clients. Wallets, she said, are “the fundamental brick on which we can build all the use cases,” and until they are universally available, the new products cannot scale.

data.title: Europe’s central bankers push for independence in payments and beyond
data.description:
Central banks need to become innovators, not just regulators.

Europe’s central banks are working to reduce the region’s dependence on others, from payment systems to cloud technology, the heads of the central banks of Germany, Spain and Denmark said at the Singapore FinTech Festival.

Joachim Nagel, president of the Deutsche Bundesbank, said Russia’s war against Ukraine was a “game changer” and an “eye-opener” that showed Europe needed to focus more on itself.

That goes beyond payments to supply chains, energy and technology, including cloud infrastructure.

“So many things where we have to do our homework, and we are currently, I believe, on a good path,” Nagel said.

Nagel described payments as critical infrastructure and, to a certain extent, a public good. The digital euro, he said, is meant to serve as a kind of digital twin to the banknotes they provide in the Eurosystem.

José Luis Escrivá, governor of the Bank of Spain, said Europe is adjusting its policies to factor in economic sovereignty.

Escrivá said competition policy has at times been short-sighted and too focused on short-term benefits for consumers, and now needs to account for the trade-offs involved.

The digital euro and the Eurosystem’s Pontes and Appia wholesale payment projects are part of that effort.

Escrivá added that with 27 member states, Europe has to build consensus at many levels. The Eurosystem has been preparing the infrastructure and running experiments for these projects whilst the regulations are still being agreed, so that both are ready at the same time.

For Ulrik Nødgaard, governor of Danmarks Nationalbank, sovereignty is about resilience and having alternatives.

Denmark’s national instant payment scheme is widely used for transfers but not in stores, where international cards and wallets dominate. Nødgaard hopes for a breakthrough next year that would let shoppers tap their phones at the supermarket using the national scheme.

“That would provide resilience. If the card rails are down, you can switch to this or the other way around,” Nødgaard said.

Sharing infrastructure can also strengthen independence, Nødgaard said. Denmark, which has its own currency pegged to the euro, decided last year to move to Europe’s TARGET settlement systems for their scale, cybersecurity and innovation.

Nødgaard said small economies have a strong case for joining forces rather than developing their own solutions.

The governors also pushed back on the idea that central banks only regulate. “We are not behind the curve in Europe, so we are innovators,” Nagel said.

Escrivá said the Bank of Spain now considers the innovative element of business models when authorising new banks and payment institutions.

Nagel added AI is changing central banking, including how monetary policy is conducted, and that whilst Europe may not have frontier AI models, it can take advantage of data from its strong industrial base.

Nødgaard said major financial innovation should be a partnership between the public and private sectors. Large-scale tokenisation, for example, needs central bank money to work.

Looking ahead, the governors pointed to AI as the next big shift. Nødgaard warned that agentic AI could make bank deposits more volatile by removing the friction of moving money between accounts, and could increase herd behaviour in markets, leading circuit breakers to be used more often.

Escrivá said regulators and financial institutions need to ensure standards keep pace with AI agents making decisions for people and firms, whilst preserving trust in money and financial stability.

“The truth is that nobody knows what is next. This is a disruptive technology. So every aspect of our life will be influenced or is already being influenced. Everything is changing. Payments is one tiny aspect of what is more or less ongoing,” Nagel said.

data.title: Payments could skip acquirers and networks in Web3 era
data.description:
Account-to-account payments will erode the four-party model of payments, said Ant International’s CEO.

The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) will erode the current four-party model of the financial system, highlighting the need to define common standards.

The current model involves the issuer, the network, the acquirer, the regulator. But that four party model may not be suitable in an era of tokenisation, blockchain, and AI, said Yang Peng, CEO of Ant International.

“When Web3 currency becomes mainstream, then we probably don’t need an acquirer, probably don’t need [a] network. It’s account-to-account. The merchant can easily process everything,” Peng said in a panel session during Singapore Fintech Festival 2026, moderated by Arjun Vir Singh, partner at Arthur D. Little.

 

Peng said that despite new business models likely emerging, the settlement and transaction rails will define responsibility.

“Once the rail and settlement layer is defined, then the game rules probably will be defined as well,” Peng said.

Javier Perez-Tasso, CEO of SWIFT, said that the market should stop pitting players against each other but realize that the future is multi-choice.

“The future is going to be multimodal, multi-rail, multi-asset,” Perez-Tasso said during the panel.

Customers demand infrastructures that provide confidence and trust, with predictability, speed, and security, Perez-Tasso said, and just technology will not be enough to provide this.

“It will take all of us to come collectively, with the public sector, with common standards, with security, resilience, governance, identity— all that are fundamental to…come up with the future of moving money across jurisdictions and currencies,” Perez-Tasso said.

Surendra Rosha, co-chief Executive, Asia and Middle East at HSBC, said that customer trust is often missing in debates about building new financial systems.

“What's missing in the debate is the customer, and the trust that the customer has in the system that allows them to then put more through that system—either keeping money with a bank like us or processing payments or other transactions through the wider ecosystem,” Rosha said.

Rosha said that it is critical that systems collectively work on retaining that trust.

For AI adoption, this meant the necessity of having human judgement and accountability, particularly in risk controls, financial crime, and sanction-related controls.

“We have to respect the fact that we are stewards of customers placing their money with us. So that creates a different level of governance of ways in which we would work versus perhaps Swift or or Ant,” Rosha said. “I think we have to respect each other's areas of expertise, but also areas of mandate.”

data.title: Singapore unveils AI missions to fight financial crime, boost SME financing
data.description:
The government will also test AI agents that can handle financial transactions.

Singapore has announced three national artificial intelligence (AI) missions to strengthen financial crime prevention, improve access to financing, and enable AI-driven transactions, said Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry Gan Kim Yong.

Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 18 November, Gan said the government would bring together financial institutions, technology companies, researchers, and public agencies to develop and test AI solutions.

The first mission focuses on detecting and preventing financial crime by allowing banks to identify suspicious transactions across multiple institutions.

“Scams are not confined within the boundary of one bank,” he said, noting that stolen funds can pass through several financial institutions within minutes.

A trial involving five banks is already underway, with their transaction data securely combined to help AI systems identify suspicious patterns that individual banks may not detect.

Meanwhile, the Monetary Authority of Singapore will begin a design study in early 2027 to develop an industry-wide scam detection system, including its governance and operating structure.

The second mission aims to improve financing access for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and startups with limited financial records or assets.

Under the initiative, AI technology companies will be invited to develop and test solutions using realistic synthetic data, whilst financial institutions and public agencies will contribute data and expertise.

SMEs will also be consulted to assess whether the solutions address their financing needs.

“Today, many lenders assess businesses largely on past performance and repayment history, and secure loans against personal guarantees and collateral,” Gan said. 

“These traditional approaches may not fully capture the creditworthiness and future potential of SMEs or newer start-ups with limited track records or assets,” he added.

The third mission focuses on enabling AI agents to carry out financial transactions on behalf of individuals and businesses, subject to defined safeguards.

The government will work with industry players to test AI agents in controlled environments, including their ability to make payments automatically once specified conditions are met.

These could include contractual payments made after agreed terms have been fulfilled and verified, or purchases completed on behalf of users.

The trials will examine safeguards covering identity verification, authorisation, accountability, and compatibility between different systems.

The Future of Finance Institute will support the three missions by coordinating industry partnerships, developing guidelines and standards, and testing solutions for wider use across the financial sector.

“Agents must operate within defined authority and limits,” Gan said, adding that institutions and businesses would remain accountable for transactions conducted on their behalf.

data.title: Singapore firms urged to go beyond efficiency and build AI-native
data.description:
Trust and talent are the two pillars needed for the shift, the Singapore DPM said.

Singapore businesses that use artificial intelligence (AI) only to improve existing operations are at the first stage of a longer journey, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said at the Singapore FinTech Festival.

Speaking in a fireside chat, Gan said most businesses are approaching AI as a way to become more efficient, effective, and competitive. Whilst he described this as the first stage most businesses go through, he said the more important shift is to build businesses with AI as their native foundation rather than as a tool layered onto what already exists.

“Today we are using AI to tell me what can I do in my business,” he said. “You need to switch it around and see how can I use AI as a native tool as a foundation to build my business.”

He used the evolution of e-commerce as an analogy. Many companies have added an e-commerce arm to existing physical operations, but a growing number of platforms have no physical shopfront and were built as digital-native businesses from the outset.

“In time to come, I think you will have many AI-native businesses built around AI,” he said.

For Singapore to reach that point, Gan identified trust as the first requirement. AI development and deployment, he said, depends on building trust with the technology, the system, and the people building the solutions. Singapore’s strength as a financial hub, he added, is itself built on its reputation as a trusted partner.

Talent is the second pillar. Gan said Singapore needs both local talent and international expertise, noting that the whole world is short of AI practitioners. He referenced the government’s Kampong AI initiative, which aims to build a community of AI talent in Singapore.

“AI talent likes to work with one another,” he said, adding that the government hopes to build “a momentum, an ecosystem, and community of AI practitioners.”

On the regional front, Gan said the signing of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement in Manila marks a significant step in regional digital economy cooperation, covering data flows and interoperability across the 11 member states. The agreement was designed as a living framework to accommodate divergent levels of digital readiness, allowing more ambitious members to pursue deeper initiatives together whilst keeping the door open for others.

Singapore takes the ASEAN chair next year and will oversee implementation. 

“We are very excited as chairman of ASEAN next year to usher it into implementation,” Gan said.

On the workforce, Gan acknowledged that anxiety amongst workers and graduates about AI’s impact on jobs is not wrong. Citing Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, he said the government’s position is that while not every job can be protected as AI changes some roles, every worker will be supported through skills upgrading and retraining.

He also addressed human oversight directly, responding to a live question from an AI agent during the fireside chat. 

“I believe strongly in AI,” he said. “I believe even stronger in human intelligence.”

data.title: Singapore banks' Q3 profit falls 10% QoQ on weaker trading income
data.description:
Non-interest income fell 19% to $4.7b as trading and investment earnings dropped 38%. 

Singapore's three major banks recorded a 10% quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) decline in combined net profit to $6.1b in the third quarter, weighed down by weaker trading and investment income, according to RHB.

Across DBS, OCBC, and UOB, income from sources other than interest fell 19% QoQ to $4.7b, driven by a 38% decline in trading, investment, and other related income.

OCBC's earnings were affected by losses on Great Eastern's bond investments, whilst UOB's previous quarter had benefited from approximately $200m in property disposal gains that did not recur.

Nevertheless, the combined net profit of the three banks rose 14% year-on-year (YoY), partly due to UOB's lower earnings in the same period last year.

Meanwhile, combined net interest income rose 3% to $8.3b, marking its first annual increase in six quarters, RHB said.

The increase was supported by loan growth of 10% YoY, with total lending across the three banks reaching $1.23t.

RHB expects the banks' combined net profit to grow 7% this year and 9% in 2027, supported by a recovery in interest margins and continued loan growth.

data.title: Easing worker fears is key to scaling artificial intelligence
data.description:
Scaling is putting manpower into what matters, said firms across four sectors.

Scaling artificial intelligence (AI) remains a distant goal for some firms, but executives said the groundwork includes allaying fears within the workforce, explaining the reasons for automation and putting manpower where it matters most.

Executives from IHH Healthcare Singapore, DHL Supply Chain Asia Pacific, FedEx, Heineken Asia Pacific and CBRE discussed AI experimentation and scaling at a panel session at the Singapore Business Review Technology Enterprise Summit.

Damien Dujacquier, managing director at management consulting firm Roland Berger, moderated the session.

IHH Healthcare Singapore uses AI in patient services, nurse rostering, and other corporate functions.

According to Roy Wee, head of digital products and services, healthcare is a very traditional and hands-on sector. AI integration involves reworking old workflows and identifying tasks that can be simplified to make way for more important work.

Patients who want water, for example, used to press the nurse call bell, and the nurse would relay the request. IHH now lets patients send such requests directly to the department concerned through an AI-enabled digital platform, Wee said.

“The nursing hours we save translate back into better clinical care for our patients. Instead of doing a housekeeping role, nurses provide more care. Again, we have no intention of cutting our nursing workforce. We want them to focus on what really matters to our patients,” he said.

DHL is deploying agentic AI in its customer service and command centres, whilst FedEx staff in its Wuhan shared service centres are adopting AI for accounting and finance work.

“We’re trying to use AI to replace repetitive work and, hopefully, get good economic value out of it,” said Michael Lai, head of service logistics, APAC, at DHL Supply Chain Asia Pacific.

Lai said business as usual (BAU) remains far off, but DHL weighs three considerations before scaling: operational fit, potential to scale and a measurable business case with a clear return on investment. He said success is judged by the benefits after deployment.

“Internally, can we save costs or find information more efficiently? And most importantly, from a customer-centricity perspective, are our customers happier, or finding information faster by calling these [AI] agents?” he said.

The firms also test deployments, using test and control groups to measure value as either growth in gross profit or savings.

At IHH Healthcare Singapore, scaling happens one hospital at a time, starting with pilots on the service side. Wee said the solutions deployed so far have saved a significant amount of nursing time.

For the executives, scaling means groundwork before technology: collecting data, reviewing processes and giving the technology time to mature whilst bringing employees on board.

Shawn Sengupta, head of digital and technology APAC at CBRE, said the company had three pieces to solve and spent six months to a year on groundwork before it began building.

“The first is data. That’s at the process level. We had to go back and look at how we actually ran our business and what the touchpoints were. … From there, we worked on things like asset data, facilities data, property data and master data across the business. … If we hadn’t done it and had started developing at scale, we would have ended up working on pilots at a smaller scale, building by building,” he said.

Rumana Rahman, vice president for human resources for APAC and MEISA at FedEx, said the company uses AI in three areas: operational optimisation, customer differentiation through predictive analytics and capability building.

“I think data is a bigger conversation than AI. I feel we give too much importance to AI, but without data, AI is nothing, in my view,” she said.

Rahman said data readiness and process readiness will remain key issues. Security will also become a bigger issue as companies scale, she said, because many AI agents cannot be fully relied on, which makes the role of regulatory bodies important.

But beyond data and efficiency, the human side remains a deciding factor.

“I think we create more anxiety for people than we should, and we have a big responsibility to first take that anxiety out and give psychological safety,” Rahman said.

She said FedEx is trying to give workers more capability and empowerment, including in its customer service and clearance centres.

“If you don’t go bottom-up, all the way, and tell people how to automate, it won’t work,” Sengupta added. He said CBRE spent a lot of time explaining the change to its product and IT teams and understanding what interested them before building began.

Rahman said capability will continue to matter, but new generations are born with AI, “I don’t think capability building is the bigger challenge. It’s adoption at scale, security and the human in the loop."

data.title: Deluge books $18.5m in orders, led by Penang data centre
data.description:
The project is due for completion by 31 March 2027.

Deluge Corporation Limited has secured about $18.5m in new contracts across Singapore and Malaysia, including a data centre project in Penang, Malaysia.

The group said the latest contract wins bring its cumulative new orders since January to more than $147.7m. 

Its outstanding order book has also surpassed $459.1m as at 17 November. 

The new contracts cover a range of infrastructure, marine and offshore, residential and industrial projects across the two markets.

The Penang project is scheduled for completion by 31 March 2027 and is expected to lift the group’s financial performance for the financial year ending 31 March 2027.

It also strengthens Deluge’s presence in Malaysia, where the group sees further opportunities to expand its footprint across the country’s growing industrial and infrastructure sectors.
